# SQS, SNS and EventBridge: questions

<!-- quiz:start id=messaging-q008 -->
### Question 1

A company processes uploaded images with Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The instances poll an Amazon SQS queue. Each message takes about the same time to process. The number of uploads changes during the day, and each image must be processed within a set time after upload. The group uses target tracking on average CPU utilization, and messages often wait too long. Which metric should the target tracking policy use to BEST meet the processing-time goal?

- The ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric of the queue alone, with one fixed target number of visible messages for the whole group.
- A metric math expression that divides ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible by GroupInServiceInstances, with the acceptable backlog per instance as the target value.
- The ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible metric of the queue, with one fixed target number of messages that the instances are processing.
- The NumberOfMessagesSent metric of the queue, with a target value that matches the average number of uploads in one minute.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** A metric math expression that divides ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible by GroupInServiceInstances, with the acceptable backlog per instance as the target value.

**Deciding phrases.** "Each message takes about the same time to process", "The number of uploads changes during the day", "BEST meet the processing-time goal"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the metric that target tracking should use to BEST meet a processing-time goal.
2. I mark the constraints: the instances poll an SQS queue, each message takes about the same time, the number of uploads changes during the day, and messages wait too long with scaling on CPU.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict the backlog per instance: the visible messages divided by the instances in service, because that number tells how long each instance needs to clear its share.
4. I remove ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible, because it counts messages that were received but not yet deleted, the work in progress. I remove NumberOfMessagesSent, because new arrivals do not show how much work waits for each instance.
5. Between the visible messages alone and the visible messages per instance the difference is the size of the group; the stem says the load changes, and the queue length might not change proportionally to the group, so I choose the backlog per instance.
6. Check: the metric math option follows the waiting work of each instance, adapts to the changing load and serves the processing-time goal. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** The goal is a wait time, and every message takes about the same time, so the signal is the waiting work of each instance. Metric math divides [ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance-metric-math) by [GroupInServiceInstances](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance-metric-math). Target tracking then keeps the [backlog per instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance) at the acceptable value as the load changes.

**Why not.**

- "The ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric of the queue alone, with ...": The queue length [might not change proportionally](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-queue-length-not-proportional) to the size of the group, so one fixed target misses the processing-time goal.
- "The ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible metric of the queue, with one ...": It counts messages [received but not yet deleted or expired](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-metric-not-visible-messages-is-in-flight): the work in progress, not the messages that wait.
- "The NumberOfMessagesSent metric of the queue, with a ...": It counts the messages that producers add to the queue, so it shows arrivals and not the waiting work of each instance.

**Twin.** If the stem said "alarm when messages wait too long" instead: [ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-metric-age-of-oldest-message-measures-lag), because it reports the oldest unprocessed message.

**Takeaway.** Scale queue workers on the backlog per instance, not on CPU or on the queue length alone.

**Review.** [Workers scale on the backlog per instance and not on queue length](2-deep.md#workers-scale-on-the-backlog-per-instance-and-not-on-queue-length-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

An Amazon SNS topic delivers messages to an Amazon SQS queue in the same AWS account. The queue's access policy allows the topic to send messages. A new company rule requires the queue to be encrypted at rest with an AWS KMS key whose key policy the company controls. After the team turned on SSE-KMS with the AWS managed key for Amazon SQS, no messages arrive in the queue. Which TWO actions will restore delivery and meet the rule with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Edit the key policy of the AWS managed key for Amazon SQS so that it allows the SNS service principal to use the key.
- Create a customer managed KMS key, and configure the queue to use this key for server-side encryption instead of the AWS managed key.
- Switch the queue to SSE-SQS encryption, which uses keys that Amazon SQS manages, and keep the access policy of the queue unchanged.
- Add a statement to the key policy of the new key that allows the SNS service principal to use kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt.
- Create a customer managed key in an AWS KMS custom key store that an AWS CloudHSM cluster backs, and configure the queue to use it.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create a customer managed KMS key, and configure the queue to use this key for server-side encryption instead of the AWS managed key.
- Add a statement to the key policy of the new key that allows the SNS service principal to use kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt.

**Deciding phrases.** "key policy the company controls", "AWS managed key for Amazon SQS", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for TWO actions that restore delivery and meet the key rule with the LEAST operational overhead.
2. I mark the constraints: SNS sends to the queue, the queue's access policy already allows the topic, the company must control the key policy, and delivery stopped after SSE-KMS with the AWS managed key.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict one fix: edit the policy of the AWS managed key so that it allows the SNS service principal.
4. I remove SSE-SQS, because the company then controls no key policy. I remove the CloudHSM custom key store, because a standard customer managed key meets the rule with less to run.
5. Between editing the AWS managed key and creating a customer managed key the difference is who owns the key policy. My first idea breaks because the key policy of the AWS managed key for Amazon SQS cannot be modified; the stem says the company controls the key policy, so I choose a customer managed key and a statement that allows SNS to use GenerateDataKey and Decrypt.
6. Check: the new key and its policy statement restore delivery, the company controls the key policy, and the access policy of the queue stays as it is. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** SNS needs the queue's KMS key to send to the encrypted queue. You [cannot modify the key policy](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-kms-aws-managed-key-policy-not-modifiable) of the AWS managed key, so the queue needs a customer managed key. Its key policy, which the company controls, must allow SNS the [API actions GenerateDataKey and Decrypt](../facts/sns.md#sns-sse-topic-to-encrypted-queue-needs-cmk-policy).

- For AWS services that send to encrypted queues, you must [create a customer managed KMS key](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-kms-service-senders-need-customer-managed-key), and the company controls its key policy.
- The key policy must grant SNS the [API actions GenerateDataKey and Decrypt](../facts/sns.md#sns-sse-topic-to-encrypted-queue-needs-cmk-policy), so that SNS can encrypt the messages that it sends.

**Why not.**

- "Edit the key policy of the AWS managed ...": You [cannot modify the key policy](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-kms-aws-managed-key-policy-not-modifiable) of the AWS managed KMS key for Amazon SQS, so no statement for SNS can be added.
- "Switch the queue to SSE-SQS encryption, which uses ...": SSE-SQS uses [SQS-managed encryption keys (SSE-SQS)](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-sse-two-key-types), so the company has no key policy to control, which the rule requires.
- "Create a customer managed key in an AWS ...": It works with the key policy statement, but a CloudHSM cluster is extra hardware to run, although a standard customer managed key meets the rule.

**Twin.** If the stem said "S3 event notifications send the messages" instead: name the S3 service principal in the key policy, because event sources need [permissions in the key policy](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-kms-service-senders-need-customer-managed-key).

**Takeaway.** An AWS service that sends to an SSE-KMS queue needs a customer managed key whose policy allows that service.

**Review.** [Resource-based policies decide which accounts and services may send to a queue](2-deep.md#resource-based-policies-decide-which-accounts-and-services-may-send-to-a-queue-4-min)

</details>

### Question 3

A company runs order-processing workers on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Several applications send messages to an Amazon SQS standard queue. The workers poll the queue and delete each message after they process it. Processing a message takes up to 4 minutes. The queue uses the default visibility timeout, and many messages are processed by two different workers. Which change will resolve this issue with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Increase the visibility timeout of the queue to a value that is longer than the longest processing time of one message.
- Create a dead-letter queue, and add a redrive policy to the queue that moves a message after several unsuccessful receives.
- Change the workers to call ChangeMessageVisibility during processing, so that each message stays hidden until the worker finishes with it.
- Change the workers to count the receives of each message and to move a message that keeps failing to a second queue.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Increase the visibility timeout of the queue to a value that is longer than the longest processing time of one message.

**Deciding phrases.** "takes up to 4 minutes", "default visibility timeout", "processed by two different workers", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Processing takes as long as 4 minutes, but the default visibility timeout is [30 seconds](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-visibility-timeout-default). If the timeout ends before the delete, the message [becomes visible again in the queue](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-undeleted-message-visible-again), and [a duplicate message is received by another consumer](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-visibility-timeout-too-short-gives-duplicate). One queue setting that is longer than the processing time keeps each message hidden until its worker deletes it.

**Why not.**

- "Create a dead-letter queue, and add a redrive ...": A dead-letter queue sets aside messages that keep failing; it does not stop a second worker from receiving a message that is still in progress.
- "Change the workers to call ChangeMessageVisibility during processing, ...": It works, but every worker needs new code for each message, although one queue setting gives the same result.
- "Change the workers to count the receives of ...": The messages do not fail; they come back because the timeout ends too early, so counting receives does not stop the duplicates.

**Twin.** If the stem said "A few malformed messages fail every time" instead: a dead-letter queue, because a redrive policy counts the [number of times a consumer can receive](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-dlq-max-receive-count-meaning) a message.

**Takeaway.** Set the visibility timeout longer than the longest processing time, or a second consumer receives the message.

**Review.** [A received message stays hidden until it is deleted or the timeout ends](2-deep.md#a-received-message-stays-hidden-until-it-is-deleted-or-the-timeout-ends-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company sends account events for many customers to Amazon SQS. The events of each customer must be processed exactly once and in the order they were sent. Events of different customers must be processed in parallel by many consumers, so that a slow customer does not delay the others. Which combination of actions should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Give each event a random message group ID, because the FIFO queue keeps one order across all of its messages.
- Use an Amazon SQS standard queue, because a standard queue delivers each message once and in the order it was sent.
- Create an Amazon SQS FIFO queue, and have the producers send the account events of all customers to that one queue.
- Create a separate Amazon SQS FIFO queue for each customer, and run a dedicated group of consumers for each of those queues.
- Set the message group ID of each event to the ID of the customer that the event belongs to.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create an Amazon SQS FIFO queue, and have the producers send the account events of all customers to that one queue.
- Set the message group ID of each event to the ID of the customer that the event belongs to.

**Deciding phrases.** "processed exactly once and in the order they were sent", "Events of different customers must be processed in parallel", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** A FIFO queue gives [exactly-once processing](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-faq-fifo-exactly-once-processing). The message group ID decides the rest: order is kept [within a message group ID](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-fifo-order-strict-within-group), and the queue allows parallel work [across different message group IDs](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-fifo-groups-processed-in-parallel). With the customer ID as the group ID, each customer keeps its order, and many consumers work on different customers at the same time.

- A FIFO queue gives [exactly-once processing](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-faq-fifo-exactly-once-processing), and one queue serves every customer without extra queues to manage.
- Order is strict [within a message group ID](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-fifo-order-strict-within-group), and different groups allow [parallel processing of messages](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-fifo-groups-processed-in-parallel) by many consumers.

**Why not.**

- "Give each event a random message group ID, ...": Order holds inside a group, but [messages with different message group IDs](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-fifo-no-order-across-groups) can arrive or be processed out of order, so random IDs break each customer's order.
- "Use an Amazon SQS standard queue, because a ...": A standard queue gives [at-least-once message delivery](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-standard-at-least-once-duplicates), so [more than one copy of a message](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-standard-at-least-once-duplicates) can arrive.
- "Create a separate Amazon SQS FIFO queue for ...": It works, but every new customer needs a new queue and new consumers, while one queue with a group for each customer does the same job.

**Twin.** If the stem said "all events must be processed in one strict order" instead: use one message group ID for all events, because order is strict [within a message group ID](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-fifo-order-strict-within-group).

**Takeaway.** In a FIFO queue, the message group ID sets the unit of order and the unit of parallel work.

**Review.** [A FIFO queue keeps order inside each message group and drops duplicates](2-deep.md#a-fifo-queue-keeps-order-inside-each-message-group-and-drops-duplicates-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A company runs an order API on Amazon EC2 instances. The API sends each order directly to the order service, which writes the order to a relational database. During sales, the database cannot keep up, requests time out, and orders are lost. Only the company's order service processes the orders. The order service must process every order, even after it has been offline for a few hours. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Have the API send each order to one Amazon SQS queue, and have each service that processes orders poll that queue and process the orders it receives.
- Have the API publish each order to an Amazon SNS topic, subscribe one Amazon SQS queue for each service that processes orders, and have each service poll its queue.
- Have the API publish each order to an Amazon SNS topic, and subscribe the HTTPS endpoint of each service that processes orders so that each service receives every order.
- Move the database to a larger instance class, and add a read replica so that the database can take more of the load during sales.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Have the API send each order to one Amazon SQS queue, and have each service that processes orders poll that queue and process the orders it receives.

**Deciding phrases.** "Only the company's order service processes the orders", "even after it has been offline for a few hours", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** One service consumes the orders, so one queue is enough. SQS is built for [buffering requests](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-decision-typical-use): the database receives orders at the pace of the order service. Each order stays in the queue [until successfully processed or expired](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-decision-keeps-until-processed), and the default retention of [4 days](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-message-retention-default) covers an outage of a few hours.

**Why not.**

- "Have the API publish each order to an ...": It works, but SNS is for [fanout notifications](../facts/sns.md#sns-decision-typical-use), and with one consumer the topic is an extra part with nothing to fan out to.
- "Have the API publish each order to an ...": In SNS, [messages are not persisted](../facts/sns.md#sns-decision-no-persistence), and HTTPS retries end within [3,600 seconds](../facts/sns.md#sns-retry-http-total-retry-time-max), so an outage of a few hours loses orders.
- "Move the database to a larger instance class, ...": A larger database still takes every write at the moment of the peak, and it holds no order while the order service is offline.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The order service, the shipping service and the analytics service must each process every order" instead: an SNS topic with one SQS queue for each service, because each queue keeps its own copy.

**Takeaway.** One consumer and a database that falls behind: put one SQS queue in front of the database.

**Review.** [SQS stores each message in several Availability Zones before the sender moves on](2-deep.md#sqs-stores-each-message-in-several-availability-zones-before-the-sender-moves-on-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A company's payment service reads orders from an Amazon SQS standard queue and charges the customer for each order. Each order has a unique order ID. Sometimes a customer is charged twice for one order. Logs show two causes: some orders are received twice from the queue, and a partner system sometimes sends the same order again several hours later. Which solution will BEST prevent duplicate charges?

- Increase the visibility timeout of the queue to its maximum value, so that a second consumer cannot receive an order that is still in progress.
- Replace the standard queue with an SQS FIFO queue that uses content-based deduplication, and keep the code of the payment service unchanged.
- Make the payment service record each order ID with a conditional write before it charges, and skip an order whose ID is already recorded.
- Keep the standard queue and fix the partner system alone, because a standard queue delivers each message exactly once and in order.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Make the payment service record each order ID with a conditional write before it charges, and skip an order whose ID is already recorded.

**Deciding phrases.** "standard queue", "sends the same order again several hours later", "BEST prevent duplicate charges"

**Why.** Duplicates come from two places, so the fix belongs in the consumer. With a standard queue you must [design your applications to be idempotent](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-faq-standard-queue-design-idempotent-consumers). A conditional write of the order ID lets the payment service charge each order a single time, whether the repeat comes from the queue or from the partner.

**Why not.**

- "Increase the visibility timeout of the queue to ...": A standard queue can deliver [more than one copy of a message](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-standard-at-least-once-duplicates) for other reasons too, and the partner repeats are new messages that no timeout stops.
- "Replace the standard queue with an SQS FIFO ...": It removes repeats only inside the [5 minute deduplication interval](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-fifo-deduplication-interval-5-minutes), so partner orders that arrive hours later are still charged twice.
- "Keep the standard queue and fix the partner ...": A standard queue gives [at-least-once message delivery](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-standard-at-least-once-duplicates), so the queue itself also repeats some orders.

**Twin.** If the stem said "all duplicates come from the queue, and the payment code cannot change" instead: a FIFO queue, because [duplicates are not introduced into the queue](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-faq-fifo-exactly-once-processing).

**Takeaway.** When duplicates come from several sources, make the consumer idempotent with a record of each processed ID.

**Review.** [A standard queue can deliver a message twice so consumers must be idempotent](2-deep.md#a-standard-queue-can-deliver-a-message-twice-so-consumers-must-be-idempotent-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A company must react whenever any Amazon EC2 instance in its AWS account changes to the stopped state. The operations team must receive an email within a few minutes, and an existing AWS Lambda function must create a ticket for each stopped instance. Instances are stopped by users in the console, by scripts and by scheduled jobs. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a Lambda function that runs every minute, calls DescribeInstances, compares the states with the last run, and sends the email and the ticket.
- Create an AWS CloudTrail trail that writes to an Amazon S3 bucket, and add an S3 event notification that invokes a function to read each log file.
- Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the StatusCheckFailed metric of each instance, and send the alarm notifications to an Amazon SNS topic with an email subscription.
- Create an Amazon EventBridge rule on the default event bus for EC2 stop events, with the Lambda function and an email-subscribed SNS topic as targets.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an Amazon EventBridge rule on the default event bus for EC2 stop events, with the Lambda function and an email-subscribed SNS topic as targets.

**Deciding phrases.** "changes to the stopped state", "an existing AWS Lambda function", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Every account has a [default event bus](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-default-bus-receives-aws-service-events) that [automatically receives events from AWS services](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-default-bus-receives-aws-service-events), and EC2 is one of those services. One rule matches the stopped state, whoever stopped the instance. A single rule can [route to multiple targets](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-faq-single-rule-routes-to-multiple-targets-in-parallel), so the topic sends the email and the function creates the ticket, with no code to poll.

**Why not.**

- "Create a Lambda function that runs every minute, ...": It works, but it is polling code to run and fix, although the default bus [automatically receives events from AWS services](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-default-bus-receives-aws-service-events).
- "Create an AWS CloudTrail trail that writes to ...": It works, but it adds a trail, a bucket and log-parsing code, which is far more to run than one rule on the event bus.
- "Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the StatusCheckFailed ...": Status checks find problems that [require your involvement to repair](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-status-check-instance-needs-you) or [require AWS involvement to repair](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-status-check-system-needs-aws); a requested stop is a state change, not a failed check.

**Twin.** If the stem said "must react when the instance health checks fail" instead: a CloudWatch alarm on StatusCheckFailed, because failed checks are a metric, not a state change.

**Takeaway.** To react to a change of an AWS resource, match its event with an EventBridge rule; do not poll.

**Review.** [An EventBridge rule matches event content and sends each match to its targets](2-deep.md#an-eventbridge-rule-matches-event-content-and-sends-each-match-to-its-targets-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A company runs order-processing workers on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Several applications send messages to an Amazon SQS standard queue. The workers poll the queue and delete each message after they process it. Processing a message takes a few seconds. A few malformed messages fail every time, and the workers receive them again and again for days. Which change will resolve this issue with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Increase the visibility timeout of the queue to a value that is longer than the longest processing time of one message.
- Create a dead-letter queue, and add a redrive policy to the queue that moves a message after several unsuccessful receives.
- Change the workers to call ChangeMessageVisibility during processing, so that each message stays hidden until the worker finishes with it.
- Change the workers to count the receives of each message and to move a message that keeps failing to a second queue.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a dead-letter queue, and add a redrive policy to the queue that moves a message after several unsuccessful receives.

**Deciding phrases.** "A few malformed messages fail every time", "again and again for days", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** A malformed message fails every time, so it returns after each visibility timeout for days. A redrive policy sets the [number of times a consumer can receive](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-dlq-max-receive-count-meaning) a message; after that, SQS moves the message to the dead-letter queue. The workers stop receiving it, and the team can review it there.

**Why not.**

- "Increase the visibility timeout of the queue to ...": A longer timeout makes the workers [wait for a relatively long time](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-visibility-timeout-too-long-delays-retry) between attempts, but the malformed message still fails and comes back.
- "Change the workers to call ChangeMessageVisibility during processing, ...": Extending the timeout from the workers delays each new attempt, but the malformed message still fails and returns to the queue.
- "Change the workers to count the receives of ...": It works, but the workers then carry custom code for what a redrive policy on the queue does without code.

**Twin.** If the stem said "many messages are processed by two different workers" instead: increase the visibility timeout, because the default of [30 seconds](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-visibility-timeout-default) ends during processing.

**Takeaway.** A message that fails every time needs a redrive policy and a dead-letter queue, not a longer timeout.

**Review.** [After too many failed receives SQS moves a message to a dead-letter queue](2-deep.md#after-too-many-failed-receives-sqs-moves-a-message-to-a-dead-letter-queue-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A company runs an order API on Amazon EC2 instances. The API sends each order directly to the order service, which writes the order to a relational database. During sales, the database cannot keep up, requests time out, and orders are lost. The order service, the shipping service and the analytics service must each process every order. Each service must process every order, even after it has been offline for a few hours. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Have the API send each order to one Amazon SQS queue, and have each service that processes orders poll that queue and process the orders it receives.
- Have the API publish each order to an Amazon SNS topic, subscribe one Amazon SQS queue for each service that processes orders, and have each service poll its queue.
- Have the API publish each order to an Amazon SNS topic, and subscribe the HTTPS endpoint of each service that processes orders so that each service receives every order.
- Move the database to a larger instance class, and add a read replica so that the database can take more of the load during sales.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Have the API publish each order to an Amazon SNS topic, subscribe one Amazon SQS queue for each service that processes orders, and have each service poll its queue.

**Deciding phrases.** "must each process every order", "even after it has been offline for a few hours", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Three services each need every order, and each can be offline for hours. Each order published to the topic is [fanned out to the SQS queues](../facts/sns.md#sns-faq-fanout-identical-messages-to-multiple-sqs-queues), one queue per service, and each queue keeps its copy until its service processes it. AWS uses this pattern to prevent message loss [when subscribers are offline](../facts/sns.md#sns-with-sqs-prevents-loss-for-offline-subscribers).

**Why not.**

- "Have the API send each order to one ...": A queue serves [a single subscriber typically](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-typically-single-subscriber-order-and-loss): three services that poll one queue split the orders, so each service misses most of them.
- "Have the API publish each order to an ...": In SNS, [messages are not persisted](../facts/sns.md#sns-decision-no-persistence), and HTTPS retries end within [3,600 seconds](../facts/sns.md#sns-retry-http-total-retry-time-max), so a service offline for hours loses orders.
- "Move the database to a larger instance class, ...": A larger database still takes every write at the moment of the peak, and it gives the shipping and analytics services no orders at all.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Only the company's order service processes the orders" instead: one SQS queue that the order service polls, because one consumer needs no topic.

**Takeaway.** Several consumers that each need every message and can go offline: SNS topic to one SQS queue each.

**Review.** [Queues subscribed to a topic give each consumer its own durable copy](2-deep.md#queues-subscribed-to-a-topic-give-each-consumer-its-own-durable-copy-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 10

A company runs an order system in which Amazon EC2 instances process messages from an Amazon SQS queue. On some nights the consumers stop working for a while, and customers notice late orders the next morning. The operations team wants to monitor the queue and receive an alarm when messages wait too long before a consumer processes them. Which Amazon CloudWatch metric should the alarm use?

- The ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible metric of the queue
- The NumberOfMessagesSent metric of the queue
- The ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage metric of the queue
- The CPUUtilization metric of the consumer instances

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** The ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage metric of the queue

**Deciding phrases.** "messages wait too long before a consumer processes them", "the consumers stop working"

**Why.** The team cares about how long messages wait, not how many arrive. [ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-metric-age-of-oldest-message-measures-lag) reports the age of the oldest unprocessed message. When the consumers stop, that age grows, so an alarm on it fires whatever the number of instances.

**Why not.**

- "The ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible metric of the queue": It counts messages [received but not yet deleted or expired](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-metric-not-visible-messages-is-in-flight), so it shows work in progress, and stopped consumers receive nothing.
- "The NumberOfMessagesSent metric of the queue": It counts the messages that producers add to the queue, so it shows arrivals, not how long any message waits.
- "The CPUUtilization metric of the consumer instances": CPU shows how busy the instances are; stopped consumers use little CPU, so the alarm stays quiet when orders wait.

**Twin.** If the stem said "scale the consumers so that the backlog stays small" instead: the [backlog per instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance), because a target tracking policy needs a value that moves with the group size.

**Takeaway.** To alarm on waiting time, watch ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage; to scale workers, use the backlog per instance.

**Review.** [Workers scale on the backlog per instance and not on queue length](2-deep.md#workers-scale-on-the-backlog-per-instance-and-not-on-queue-length-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 11

A company is building an event-driven platform for its online store. Services that several teams own must react to events, and each service needs only some of the events. The teams do not want to write or run routing code. The events come from AWS services, from the company's own applications, and from a SaaS partner's application. Each service selects events by fields inside the event detail. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Write the events to an Amazon Kinesis data stream, and have every service read all records of the stream and discard the events that it does not need.
- Send the events to one Amazon SQS queue, and have every service poll the queue and discard the events that it does not need.
- Send the events to an Amazon EventBridge event bus, and create one rule for each service with an event pattern that matches the events it needs.
- Publish the events to an Amazon SNS topic, and subscribe each service to the topic with a filter policy that matches the events it needs.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Send the events to an Amazon EventBridge event bus, and create one rule for each service with an event pattern that matches the events it needs.

**Deciding phrases.** "from a SaaS partner's application", "by fields inside the event detail", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The SaaS source decides it: EventBridge is the [only event-based service](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-faq-eventbridge-only-service-integrating-directly-with-saas-partners) that integrates directly with [third-party SaaS partners](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-faq-eventbridge-only-service-integrating-directly-with-saas-partners). The [default event bus](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-default-bus-receives-aws-service-events) also [automatically receives events from AWS services](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-default-bus-receives-aws-service-events), and a rule for each service selects events by fields in the event detail, with no routing code.

**Why not.**

- "Write the events to an Amazon Kinesis data ...": A stream is built for [real-time processing of streaming big data](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-faq-kinesis-streams-realtime-and-replay); every service would need its own code to read and filter events that a rule matches for it.
- "Send the events to one Amazon SQS queue, ...": A queue serves [a single subscriber typically](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-typically-single-subscriber-order-and-loss): services that poll one queue split the events, so each service misses events it needs.
- "Publish the events to an Amazon SNS topic, ...": EventBridge is the [only event-based service](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-faq-eventbridge-only-service-integrating-directly-with-saas-partners) with a direct SaaS partner link, so the SaaS events would need extra parts before they reach the topic.

**Twin.** If the stem said "All events come from the company's own order application. Every event must also reach the mobile phones of thousands of field agents by SMS" instead: an SNS topic with filter policies.

**Takeaway.** Events from AWS services, your applications and SaaS partners, matched on content: an EventBridge event bus with rules.

**Review.** [An EventBridge rule matches event content and sends each match to its targets](2-deep.md#an-eventbridge-rule-matches-event-content-and-sends-each-match-to-its-targets-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 12

A company uses an Amazon SQS standard queue with a dead-letter queue. Both queues keep the default message retention period. A message moves to the dead-letter queue after it fails several times, usually within one hour of the first send. Failed messages disappear from the dead-letter queue before the support team reviews them. The company must retain each failed message for at least 10 days after it was first sent. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Set the message retention period of the source queue to 14 days, and keep the retention period of the dead-letter queue at its default.
- Set the message retention period of the dead-letter queue to 14 days, and keep the retention period of the source queue unchanged.
- Lower the maximum receives of the redrive policy, so that failed messages move sooner and get more time in the dead-letter queue.
- Create a scheduled AWS Lambda function that copies the messages in the dead-letter queue to an Amazon S3 bucket every day.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Set the message retention period of the dead-letter queue to 14 days, and keep the retention period of the source queue unchanged.

**Deciding phrases.** "Both queues keep the default message retention period", "at least 10 days after it was first sent", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** In a standard queue, [the enqueue timestamp is unchanged](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-dlq-standard-enqueue-timestamp-unchanged) when a message moves, so the dead-letter queue counts its retention from the first send. Its default of [4 days](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-message-retention-default) is too short. AWS advises a dead-letter queue retention [longer than the retention period](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-dlq-retention-longer-than-source-queue) of the source queue, and the maximum of [14 days](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-message-retention-range) covers 10 days.

**Why not.**

- "Set the message retention period of the source ...": The messages leave the source queue within an hour; the dead-letter queue still deletes them [4 days](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-message-retention-default) after the first send.
- "Lower the maximum receives of the redrive policy, ...": In a standard queue [the enqueue timestamp is unchanged](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-dlq-standard-enqueue-timestamp-unchanged) by the move, so an earlier move gives no extra time.
- "Create a scheduled AWS Lambda function that copies ...": It works, but the company writes and runs copy code when one queue setting keeps the messages long enough.

**Twin.** If the stem said "for at least 30 days after it was first sent" instead: copy the failed messages to Amazon S3, because a queue keeps a message for at most [14 days](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-message-retention-range).

**Takeaway.** A dead-letter queue counts retention from the first send, so give it the longer retention.

**Review.** [After too many failed receives SQS moves a message to a dead-letter queue](2-deep.md#after-too-many-failed-receives-sqs-moves-a-message-to-a-dead-letter-queue-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=messaging-q017 -->
### Question 13

A company publishes order events to a custom Amazon EventBridge event bus. A rule on the bus sends the events to an AWS Lambda function. Last week, a bug made the function process orders wrongly for several hours. After the fix, the company could not process those events again. After any future bug, the company must be able to process the events of the last 30 days again. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

- After each fix, configure the Lambda function to read the events of the affected time window again from the custom event bus.
- Configure an Amazon SQS dead-letter queue for the rule target, and after each fix send the events in that dead-letter queue to the function again.
- Add a rule that sends every event through Amazon Data Firehose to Amazon S3, and write a tool that publishes the stored events again.
- Create an archive of the event bus that keeps events for 30 days, and after each fix start a replay of the affected time window.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an archive of the event bus that keeps events for 30 days, and after each fix start a replay of the affected time window.

**Deciding phrases.** "process orders wrongly for several hours", "process the events of the last 30 days again", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The bus keeps nothing by itself: EventBridge [doesn't persist events](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-decision-no-persistence-at-least-once). An archive keeps them, and you set the [days to retain events in the archive](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-archive-retention-indefinite-by-default). After a fix, a replay lets you [reprocess past events](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-faq-event-replay-reprocesses-past-events-to-bus-or-rule) of the affected window, and the rule sends them to the fixed function.

**Why not.**

- "After each fix, configure the Lambda function to ...": EventBridge [doesn't persist events](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-decision-no-persistence-at-least-once), so the bus has no past events for the function to read.
- "Configure an Amazon SQS dead-letter queue for the ...": A target's dead-letter queue stores [events that couldn't successfully be delivered](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-dlq-is-standard-sqs-queue); these events were delivered, and the function processed them wrongly.
- "Add a rule that sends every event through ...": It works, but the company builds and runs a copy pipeline and a resend tool that an archive and a replay already provide.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the rule could not deliver the events to the function" instead: a dead-letter queue on the target, because it stores [events that couldn't successfully be delivered](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-dlq-is-standard-sqs-queue).

**Takeaway.** To process EventBridge events again later, archive them first and replay them after the fix.

**Review.** [Failed deliveries are retried and then dropped unless a dead-letter queue catches them](2-deep.md#failed-deliveries-are-retried-and-then-dropped-unless-a-dead-letter-queue-catches-them-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=messaging-q019 -->
### Question 14

An Amazon SNS standard topic delivers order events to a partner's HTTPS endpoint and to an Amazon SQS queue of the company. The partner endpoint is sometimes unavailable for several hours, and the events for the partner are lost. The company must keep each undelivered event for the partner so that it can send the event again later. Which combination of actions meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Attach an Amazon SQS queue as the dead-letter queue of the SNS topic itself, so that the queue catches the failed deliveries of every subscription of the topic.
- Create an Amazon SQS standard queue in the same AWS account and Region as the partner's subscription, with a policy that allows the topic to send.
- Change the delivery policy of the HTTPS subscription so that Amazon SNS keeps retrying each failed delivery to the partner endpoint for 24 hours.
- Replace the HTTPS subscription with an AWS Lambda function that calls the partner endpoint and stores each failed event in Amazon S3.
- Attach an Amazon SQS standard queue as the dead-letter queue of the partner's HTTPS subscription, and send the stored events again when the partner is back.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create an Amazon SQS standard queue in the same AWS account and Region as the partner's subscription, with a policy that allows the topic to send.
- Attach an Amazon SQS standard queue as the dead-letter queue of the partner's HTTPS subscription, and send the stored events again when the partner is back.

**Deciding phrases.** "unavailable for several hours", "keep each undelivered event for the partner", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** When its retries end, SNS [stops retrying the delivery and discards the message](../facts/sns.md#sns-retry-exhausted-discards-unless-dlq) unless [a dead-letter queue is attached to the subscription](../facts/sns.md#sns-retry-exhausted-discards-unless-dlq). So the company creates a standard queue that SNS can write to and attaches it to the partner's subscription. The queue keeps each undelivered event until the company sends it again.

- The dead-letter queue must be in the [same AWS account and Region](../facts/sns.md#sns-dlq-same-account-and-region-as-subscription) as the subscription, and SNS sends to it after you [set a policy on the Amazon SQS queue](../facts/sns.md#sns-sqs-queue-needs-policy-allowing-topic).
- Deliveries happen per subscription, so the dead-letter queue is [attached to an Amazon SNS subscription](../facts/sns.md#sns-dlq-attached-to-subscription-not-topic) and keeps the partner's failed events for a later resend.

**Why not.**

- "Attach an Amazon SQS queue as the dead-letter ...": A topic has no dead-letter queue, because [message deliveries happen at the subscription level](../facts/sns.md#sns-dlq-attached-to-subscription-not-topic).
- "Change the delivery policy of the HTTPS subscription ...": The total retry time of an HTTP/S delivery policy cannot exceed [3,600 seconds](../facts/sns.md#sns-retry-http-total-retry-time-max), so the topic cannot hold an event for a whole day.
- "Replace the HTTPS subscription with an AWS Lambda ...": It works, but the company writes and runs delivery and retry code that a dead-letter queue on the subscription already gives.

**Twin.** If the stem said "each event must wait in a queue until the partner pulls it" instead: subscribe an SQS queue for the partner, which prevents loss [when subscribers are offline](../facts/sns.md#sns-with-sqs-prevents-loss-for-offline-subscribers).

**Takeaway.** An SNS dead-letter queue belongs to one subscription, in the same account and Region.

**Review.** [Failed deliveries are retried and then dropped unless a dead-letter queue catches them](2-deep.md#failed-deliveries-are-retried-and-then-dropped-unless-a-dead-letter-queue-catches-them-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=messaging-q021 -->
### Question 15

A company runs the sign-up process of its web application on AWS Lambda. The company must send a reminder email to each new user 3 days after the user signs up. Each reminder is a one-time action for that user, and many users sign up every day. An existing Lambda function already sends one reminder email when it is invoked with a user ID. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- When a user signs up, send the user ID to an Amazon SQS delay queue with a delay of 3 days, and have the reminder function read the queue.
- Run a cron job on an Amazon EC2 instance every hour that reads the user table and invokes the reminder function for users who signed up 3 days ago.
- When a user signs up, create an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler one-time schedule that invokes the reminder function with the user ID 3 days later.
- When a user signs up, send the user ID to an Amazon SQS queue with a message timer of 3 days, and have the reminder function read the queue.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** When a user signs up, create an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler one-time schedule that invokes the reminder function with the user ID 3 days later.

**Deciding phrases.** "3 days after the user signs up", "one-time action", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** SQS delay queues and message timers schedule delivery [up to 15 minutes in the future](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-eventbridge-scheduler-for-advanced-scheduling), far short of 3 days. For longer waits, [EventBridge Scheduler is the recommended solution](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-eventbridge-scheduler-for-advanced-scheduling). A one-time schedule per user [invokes a target only once](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-scheduler-one-time-schedule-invokes-once), at the reminder time, and nothing runs in between.

**Why not.**

- "When a user signs up, send the user ...": A delay queue holds a message for at most [15 minutes](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-delay-queue-range), so a delay of 3 days is not possible.
- "Run a cron job on an Amazon EC2 ...": It works, but the company patches and runs an instance and writes scanning code for a job that a schedule does by itself.
- "When a user signs up, send the user ...": A message timer has the same limit as a delay queue: at most [15 minutes](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-message-timer-range) for each message.

**Twin.** If the stem said "10 minutes after the user signs up" instead: an SQS delay queue fits, because it delays delivery for at most [15 minutes](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-delay-queue-range).

**Takeaway.** A wait longer than [15 minutes](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-delay-queue-range) is a job for EventBridge Scheduler, not for an SQS delay.

**Review.** [An EventBridge rule matches event content and sends each match to its targets](2-deep.md#an-eventbridge-rule-matches-event-content-and-sends-each-match-to-its-targets-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 16

A company is building an event-driven platform for its online store. Services that several teams own must react to events, and each service needs only some of the events. The teams do not want to write or run routing code. All events come from the company's own order application. Every event must also reach the mobile phones of thousands of field agents by SMS within seconds. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Write the events to an Amazon Kinesis data stream, and have every service read all records of the stream and discard the events that it does not need.
- Send the events to one Amazon SQS queue, and have every service poll the queue and discard the events that it does not need.
- Send the events to an Amazon EventBridge event bus, and create one rule for each service with an event pattern that matches the events it needs.
- Publish the events to an Amazon SNS topic, and subscribe each service to the topic with a filter policy that matches the events it needs.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Publish the events to an Amazon SNS topic, and subscribe each service to the topic with a filter policy that matches the events it needs.

**Deciding phrases.** "All events come from the company's own order application", "mobile phones of thousands of field agents by SMS", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** One service covers both needs. An SNS topic delivers to [mobile applications, mobile phone numbers, and email addresses](../facts/sns.md#sns-a2p-subscriber-types) as well as to services, and SNS is recommended for [thousands or millions of endpoints](../facts/sns.md#sns-faq-sns-recommended-for-high-fan-out-thousands-or-millions). Each service picks its events with a filter policy, and the field agents' phones receive every event.

**Why not.**

- "Write the events to an Amazon Kinesis data ...": A stream is built for [real-time processing of streaming big data](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-faq-kinesis-streams-realtime-and-replay); each service needs its own filter code, and the SMS messages still need another service.
- "Send the events to one Amazon SQS queue, ...": A queue serves [a single subscriber typically](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-typically-single-subscriber-order-and-loss): services that poll one queue split the events, and a queue sends no SMS.
- "Send the events to an Amazon EventBridge event ...": It works for the services, but the SMS messages still need an SNS topic as a rule target: two services where SNS alone covers both needs.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The events come from AWS services, from the company's own applications, and from a SaaS partner's application" instead: an EventBridge event bus, because it integrates directly with [third-party SaaS partners](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-faq-eventbridge-only-service-integrating-directly-with-saas-partners).

**Takeaway.** Events from your own application that also go to many phones: an SNS topic with filter policies.

**Review.** [An SNS topic pushes each published message to all its subscribers](2-deep.md#an-sns-topic-pushes-each-published-message-to-all-its-subscribers-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 17

A company publishes every order event to an Amazon SNS standard topic. Each message has a message attribute that holds the order type. Two Amazon SQS queues are subscribed to the topic. A Lambda function is also subscribed: it receives every event and copies the return events into a third queue, the returns queue. The company wants to remove the function, and the returns queue must still receive only the return events. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

- Subscribe the returns queue to the topic directly, and give that subscription a filter policy that matches the order type of return events.
- Keep a Lambda function between the topic and the returns queue, because an SNS topic sends every message to every subscription.
- Create a separate SNS topic for each order type, change the publishers to send each event to its topic, and subscribe the returns queue to one.
- Replace the topic with an Amazon EventBridge event bus, create one rule for each queue, and change the publishers to send events to the bus.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Subscribe the returns queue to the topic directly, and give that subscription a filter policy that matches the order type of return events.

**Deciding phrases.** "message attribute that holds the order type", "remove the function", "LEAST development effort"

**Why.** Subscribers can [selectively receive only a subset](../facts/sns.md#sns-faq-message-filtering-subscribers-receive-subset) of the topic's messages. The order type is already a message attribute, so a filter policy on the returns queue's subscription does the function's work. The publishers, the topic and the other two queues do not change.

**Why not.**

- "Keep a Lambda function between the topic and ...": A subscriber gets every message by default, but you can [assign a filter policy to the topic subscription](../facts/sns.md#sns-filter-default-every-message) instead of a function.
- "Create a separate SNS topic for each order ...": It works, but every publisher changes, although one filter policy on a subscription to the existing topic gives the same result.
- "Replace the topic with an Amazon EventBridge event ...": It works, but publishers and consumers move to a new service, although the topic already offers [subscription filter policies](../facts/sns.md#sns-decision-filter-policies).

**Twin.** If the stem said "events also come from a SaaS partner application" instead: an EventBridge event bus with rules, because EventBridge integrates directly with [third-party SaaS partners](../facts/eventbridge.md#eventbridge-faq-eventbridge-only-service-integrating-directly-with-saas-partners).

**Takeaway.** To give one subscriber a subset of a topic's messages, put a filter policy on its subscription.

**Review.** [A filter policy decides which messages reach each subscription](2-deep.md#a-filter-policy-decides-which-messages-reach-each-subscription-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 18

An application in account B runs on Amazon EC2 instances with an IAM role. The role's identity-based policy allows sqs:SendMessage on an Amazon SQS queue in account A. Every SendMessage call fails with an access denied error. The queue uses SSE-SQS encryption, and its access policy has not changed since the queue was created. Which solution grants access in the MOST secure way and follows the principle of least privilege?

- Add a statement to the queue's access policy in account A that allows the role's ARN to call sqs:SendMessage on this queue.
- Change the identity-based policy of the role in account B to allow sqs:* on all resources, so that the role can reach the queue.
- Add a statement to the queue's access policy in account A that allows every principal (*) to call sqs:SendMessage on this queue.
- Add a statement to the queue's access policy that allows the role's ARN, and remove sqs:SendMessage from the role's own policy.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add a statement to the queue's access policy in account A that allows the role's ARN to call sqs:SendMessage on this queue.

**Deciding phrases.** "An application in account B", "queue in account A", "its access policy has not changed", "MOST secure"

**Why.** The role already has its allow in account B. The queue's policy [allows only the queue owner](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-default-access-policy-owner-only), so account A still denies the call. Account A must [configure the queue's access policy](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-cross-account-needs-queue-access-policy) to allow that principal, and a statement that names one role and one action grants exactly what the application needs.

**Why not.**

- "Change the identity-based policy of the role in ...": Account A must [configure the queue's access policy](../facts/sqs.md#sqs-cross-account-needs-queue-access-policy) for the role, and sqs:* on every resource also breaks least privilege.
- "Add a statement to the queue's access policy ...": It works, but a wildcard principal lets principals of every AWS account send to the queue, which breaks least privilege.
- "Add a statement to the queue's access policy ...": AWS [allows the request only if both evaluations return Allow](../facts/iam.md#iam-eval-cross-account-needs-both-policies), so the role's own permission must stay.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the queue is in the same account as the role" instead: the call already succeeds, because [the permissions of identity-based and resource-based policies are a union](../facts/iam.md#iam-eval-same-account-identity-or-resource-allow).

**Takeaway.** Cross-account access to a queue needs the queue's access policy to allow the principal, as well as the principal's own policy.

**Review.** [Resource-based policies decide which accounts and services may send to a queue](2-deep.md#resource-based-policies-decide-which-accounts-and-services-may-send-to-a-queue-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->
